```{r setup}
# library(pitw)
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
.gg_pedantic(size = 0.5)
set.seed(1001)
```

Everything else in this package asks whether a forecaster's stated uncertainty
is the right *size*. This vignette asks a different question: what happens when
it is the right size but the wrong *shape*?

A forecaster that reports a normal distribution for a quantity whose errors are
log-normal is not miscalibrated in the dispersion sense — its median is right
and its interval widths are right on average. It is **misspecified**: it has
assumed the wrong distributional family. Positive, skewed quantities such as
incidence, $R_t$ or any rate are routinely reported with symmetric intervals,
so this is a common failure in practice and not a contrived one.

The questions are:

1. Do the metrics detect a pure family mismatch at all?
2. Can they tell it apart from a genuine dispersion error?
3. Does the bias adjustment still work when the error distribution is skewed?
   The adjustment is median-based, which *should* make it robust to asymmetry,
   but that has been an argument rather than a result.

# 1. Constructing a pure shape mismatch

To isolate shape we must hold everything else fixed, which the package's
four-parameter families make straightforward: `norm4`, `lnorm4` and `gamma4`
are all parametrised by a **median** and a **coefficient of variation**
$\kappa$. Matching both leaves only the shape to differ.

The construction uses the fact that `lnorm4` and `gamma4` are scale families.
Draw a multiplicative error $w_i \sim \mathcal{T}(\text{median}=1, \kappa)$
from the *true* family $\mathcal{T}$, and place the forecast at
$\ell_i = x/w_i$. Then

$$
x \;=\; \ell_i w_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{T}(\text{median}=\ell_i,\ \kappa)
$$

so a forecaster reporting $\mathcal{T}(\ell_i, \kappa)$ is **exactly
calibrated** by construction. A forecaster reporting a different family
$\mathcal{R}(\ell_i, \kappa)$ — same median, same coefficient of variation — is
wrong in shape and in nothing else.

```{r construction}
# One estimator: n predictions of a true value of 1, errors from `truth`,
# predictive distribution reported as `report`.
misspecified <- function(truth, report, kappa, kappa_reported = kappa,
                         bias = 1, n = 2000) {
  w <- rlang::as_function(sprintf("r%s", truth))(n, 1, kappa)
  pit_w(rep(1, n), bias / w, kappa_reported, dist = report, link = "log")
}
```

The whole argument rests on the three families agreeing about what a median
and a coefficient of variation mean, so it is worth confirming that each one
inverts correctly before relying on any of it:

```{r roundtrip}
map_dfr(c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"), function(f) {
  q <- rlang::as_function(sprintf("q%s", f))(0.9, 2, 0.5)
  tibble(family = f, q90 = q,
         recovered_p = rlang::as_function(sprintf("p%s", f))(q, 2, 0.5))
})
```

A quick sanity check that the construction does what it claims — reporting the
true family should score at the null level, which at $n = 2000$ is a $B_{pit}$
of about `r round(sqrt(2 * pi) / 8 / sqrt(2000), 4)`:

```{r sanity}
map_dfr(c(0.3, 0.6, 1.0), function(k) {
  misspecified("gamma4", "gamma4", k) |> mutate(kappa = k)
}) |>
  transmute(kappa, B_pit, U_pit, D_pit)
```

# 2. Three kinds of mismatch

We sweep $\kappa$ from 0.01 (nearly symmetric, where all three families almost
coincide) to 0.8 (strongly skewed, where they do not), for two true families
and three reported ones. Twenty replicate estimators per point.

```{r sweep}
grid <- crossing(
  truth  = c("gamma4", "lnorm4"),
  report = c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"),
  kappa  = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8),
  rep    = 1:20
)

sweep <- grid |>
  mutate(score = pmap(list(truth, report, kappa),
                      ~ misspecified(..1, ..2, ..3))) |>
  unnest(score) |>
  mutate(match = if_else(truth == report, "correct family", "misspecified"))

summ <- sweep |>
  group_by(truth, report, kappa, match) |>
  summarise(across(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), median), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r sweep-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
crit <- tibble(
  metric = c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"),
  critical = c(b_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05,
               u_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05,
               d_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05)
)

summ |>
  pivot_longer(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(kappa, value, colour = report, linetype = match)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(data = crit, aes(yintercept = critical),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = filter(crit, metric == "D_pit"),
             aes(yintercept = -critical),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ truth, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(truth = ~ paste("true family:", .x))) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("coefficient of variation  ", kappa)),
       y = NULL, colour = "reported as", linetype = NULL)
```

Three things to read off.

**The metrics do detect it.** Every misspecified curve leaves its critical
value, and does so at a $\kappa$ of around 0.4 — well inside the range of real
skewed quantities. At $\kappa = 0.2$ the families are close enough that nothing
fires, correctly: a mismatch that makes no practical difference is not
reported as one.

**The direction of the gamma/log-normal mismatch is signed and
interpretable.** Reporting log-normal when the truth is gamma gives a
*positive* $D_{pit}$; reporting gamma when the truth is log-normal gives a
*negative* one. The log-normal has the heavier right tail, so using it where it
does not belong puts too much mass in the tail — conservative — and the metric
says so with a sign.

**Reporting a normal behaves differently.** $D_{pit}$ stays near zero for both
true families, while $U_{pit}$ rises steeply. That is the "right width, wrong
shape" signature from the three-part test, and it is exactly what should
happen: a symmetric distribution fitted to a skewed one is too light on one
side and too heavy on the other, and those two errors cancel in the signed
metric.

# 3. Telling shape from width

That last observation generalises into a usable diagnostic. Compare the
undirected and directed metrics as a ratio, $U_{pit}/|D_{pit}|$, against a
reference: a forecaster with the **right family but the wrong width**.

```{r ratio}
width_error <- crossing(kappa_reported = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9), rep = 1:20) |>
  mutate(score = map(kappa_reported, ~ misspecified("gamma4", "gamma4", 0.6, .x))) |>
  unnest(score) |>
  transmute(scenario = "wrong width, right family", U_pit, D_pit)

shape_error <- sweep |>
  filter(match == "misspecified", kappa >= 0.6) |>
  transmute(scenario = if_else(report == "norm4",
                               "wrong skew (normal reported)",
                               "wrong tail (gamma/lnorm swapped)"),
            U_pit, D_pit)

bind_rows(width_error, shape_error) |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(median_U = median(U_pit),
            median_abs_D = median(abs(D_pit)),
            ratio = median(U_pit / abs(D_pit)))
```

```{r ratio-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
bind_rows(width_error, shape_error) |>
  ggplot(aes(abs(D_pit), U_pit, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = expression(paste("|", D[pit], "|")), y = expression(U[pit]),
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

A **pure width error sits on the diagonal**: $U_{pit} = |D_{pit}|$ almost
exactly, because stating intervals uniformly too narrow pushes the PIT values
toward both ends in a way that the signed weight accumulates rather than
cancels.

A **tail-weight mismatch also sits on the diagonal.** Swapping gamma for
log-normal at matched median and $\kappa$ is, as far as the PIT values are
concerned, indistinguishable from getting the width wrong. This is an honest
negative result and worth stating plainly: the metrics measure dispersion
calibration *as realised*, and a forecaster can achieve the realised effect of
an over-wide interval either by stating one or by choosing a family with too
heavy a tail. No PIT-based diagnostic can separate those, because the PIT
values are identical.

A **skew mismatch sits well above the diagonal**, with ratios of 3–20. Fitting
a symmetric family to a skewed one produces a departure the signed metric
cancels, so $U_{pit} \gg |D_{pit}|$.

So the practical rule is the one the three-part test already implies, now with
a concrete cause attached:

| Pattern | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| $U_{pit} \approx \lvert D_{pit}\rvert$, both significant | net dispersion error — stated width wrong, **or** tail weight wrong |
| $U_{pit} \gg \lvert D_{pit}\rvert$ | asymmetry mismatch — a symmetric family fitted to a skewed quantity |
| only $B_{pit}$ significant | location error, family and width fine |

# 4. Does the bias adjustment survive asymmetry?

The adjustment estimates a single link-scale shift using a **median**, which
should make it robust to skew where a mean-based estimator would not be. With
a log link, a bias is a multiplicative factor, so we scale every forecast by
$b$ and watch what happens.

```{r bias-invariance}
bias_sweep <- crossing(
  report = c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"),
  bias   = c(1, 1.25, 1.6, 2),
  rep    = 1:20
) |>
  mutate(score = pmap(list(report, bias),
                      ~ misspecified("gamma4", ..1, 0.6, bias = ..2))) |>
  unnest(score)

bias_sweep |>
  group_by(report, bias) |>
  summarise(across(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), median), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bias, values_from = c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit))
```

```{r bias-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
bias_sweep |>
  pivot_longer(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(bias), value, colour = report, fill = report)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_boxplot(outliers = FALSE, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "multiplicative bias", y = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

$B_{pit}$ climbs steeply with the bias, as it must — the forecasts really are
displaced. $U_{pit}$ and $D_{pit}$ are **flat**: the same values at a bias of 2
as at no bias at all, for every reported family including the misspecified
ones.

So the claim holds. The median-based adjustment is bias-invariant under skewed
error distributions, not only under the symmetric ones the main validation uses,
and the invariance is not disturbed by the family being wrong at the same time.
That matters because misspecification and bias are exactly the pair you expect
to co-occur in practice: a model that has the wrong family for a skewed
quantity is also likely to be systematically off-centre.

# 5. Summary and caveats

- A pure family mismatch — right median, right coefficient of variation, wrong
  shape — **is** detected, from around $\kappa \approx 0.4$ upward.
- A **tail-weight** mismatch is indistinguishable from a width error, because
  it produces the same PIT values. The metrics report the net realised
  dispersion error, which is the honest answer to the question they are asked.
- A **skew** mismatch has its own signature, $U_{pit} \gg |D_{pit}|$, which no
  width error produces.
- The median-based bias adjustment remains exactly bias-invariant under skewed
  errors, including when the predictive family is simultaneously wrong.

Caveats. All of this holds the median and coefficient of variation matched exactly; a real misspecified model usually gets those slightly wrong too, so
the signatures above will be mixed rather than pure. The families compared here
are the realistic ones for positive skewed quantities, and nothing is claimed
about heavy-tailed symmetric alternatives such as a $t$ distribution, which the
package does not currently provide in the four-parameter form. And a normal
family fitted to a positive quantity places mass below zero; at the larger
$\kappa$ values here that is part of what is being detected, which is realistic
but means the effect is not purely one of skew.
